description: We are passionate and innovative team of students interested in space technology, artificial intelligence, software development, and scientific research. Our goal is to transform creative ideas into practical solutions.
summary:
Horizon Line is a free web app that answers two questions for any lunar south pole site and date: when do you have sunlight, and when can you call home? At the south pole the Sun never rises more than about 1.5° above a flat horizon, and Earth stays within a few degrees of the horizon too. So a crater rim kilometres away decides power and direct-to-Earth (DTE) radio. Existing tools give exact answers but need specialists.
We cast 720 rays (one every 0.5°) across NASA LRO LOLA terrain to build each site's real horizon. We combine it with hourly Sun and Earth positions from NASA/JPL SPICE (DE440), and check the Moon's visibility from the Deep Space Network. The app has four tools: a Power & Comms Calendar (sunlit %, Earth %, time to sunset/Earthset, longest dark stretch), Site Duel, Window Finder (e.g. "6 days with Sun and Earth up") and Classroom Mode. It covers all nine Artemis III candidate regions and any clicked point. Our ephemeris matches JPL Horizons to 0.001°, and our 18.6-year sunlight percentages are within 3 points of NASA's published LOLA illumination maps at 8 of 10 test points.
details:
What it does. Horizon Line is a browser-based mission-analysis tool for the lunar south pole. You pick one of the nine NASA Artemis III candidate regions, or click any point on a south pole illumination map, and choose a date and time between 2026 and 2030. The app shows:

Horizon Ring and Panorama: the site's 360° terrain horizon, with the Sun's and Earth's paths over a lunar month. It gives Sun elevation and azimuth, the percentage of the solar disc visible, how far the Sun clears the terrain, time until sunset or sunrise and Earthset or Earthrise, and which NASA Deep Space Network complexes (Goldstone DSS-14, Madrid DSS-63, Canberra DSS-43) can see the Moon.

Power & Comms Calendar: a 30-day hourly strip with sunlit %, Earth-in-view %, both together, Earth + DSN %, the longest dark stretch that batteries must survive, and the longest Earth outage.

Site Duel: two sites over the same dates, with the winner marked on each metric. There is no arbitrary combined score.

Window Finder: mission rules such as "6 days with ≥50% of the Sun's disc and Earth in view (and DSN)". The 6-day default matches the ~5.75–6.25-day Artemis III surface stay. It scans five years and returns ranked windows, or says plainly that none exist.

Classroom Mode: a plain-language explanation that updates as you move a time slider, with a play button and a 0–10 m mast slider, so students can see why the pole has endless grazing sunrise.

Custom coordinates: click the map or type a latitude and longitude. The 720-ray horizon is computed in your browser, and the point can be shared as a link.

How it works.

Terrain: NASA LRO LOLA polar DEMs (80 m and 120 m per pixel) from the PDS Geosciences Node, in the MOON_ME frame on a 1737.4 km sphere.

Horizon: from each site we cast 720 great-circle rays (one every 0.5° of azimuth) out to 150 km. The elevation angle of each terrain point includes lunar curvature: θ = atan2(r_t·cos ψ − r_obs, r_t·sin ψ). The highest angle on each ray is the horizon. The Moon has no atmosphere, so there is no refraction. Masks are computed for mast heights of 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 m.

Ephemeris: hourly Sun and Earth vectors from NASA/JPL NAIF SPICE (DE440 and the DE440 lunar orientation, MOON_ME frame, light-time and aberration corrected), 2026–2030. The browser converts them to local azimuth and elevation at the site.

Visibility: a body is visible when it is above the terrain at its azimuth. For the Sun we compute the fraction of the disc that is visible. For DTE we also require at least one DSN complex to see the Moon at 10° or higher.

Scores: the visibility results feed the calendar, duel and window search.

Validation (our own comparisons with public NASA products, not a NASA certification).

Ephemeris against JPL Horizons: Sun and Earth azimuth and elevation agree to about 0.001°. The Moon's elevation from the DSN stations matches Horizons too.

Terrain against NASA PGDA Product 69 (Mazarico et al. 2011): we simulated 18.6 years hourly. Our sunlit % is within 3 points of the published map at 8 of 10 points, and our Earth-visibility % is within 3.6 points at all 10. Malapert is 6 points low, which we explain as 80 m terrain blunting a sharp summit.

Resolution sensitivity: with 20 m terrain, slopes within about 100 m of the exact spot can change sunlight by up to 20 points at mast 0. The exact placement of a lander or mast matters.

Benefits and impact. Mission planners get a first-pass site and date screen in minutes instead of setting up SPICE and terrain pipelines. When a launch slips they can see straight away how a new date or a site a few kilometres away changes power and comms. Lander and rover teams get the longest-night figure for battery sizing. Educators and the public get an interactive, honest picture of why the south pole is chosen and why landing windows are narrow. All horizon masks are open data (CC0) and the code is MIT licensed.

Tools. Python (NumPy, SciPy, SpiceyPy) for the offline pipeline; TypeScript, React and Vite for the web app; SVG for the visualisations; GitHub and GitHub Pages for hosting. No server or login is needed.

Creativity. The "Horizon Ring" turns a whole site's power and comms geometry into one picture. The time-to-sunset and Earthset countdowns, the per-metric Site Duel and the rule-based Window Finder answer the questions planners actually ask. Classroom Mode reuses the same real data instead of a simplified simulation.

Factors we considered. We used real NASA data only. Visibility is labelled as geometric: sunlight is not power and Earth in view is not a radio link. We disclose limits (80–120 m terrain misses boulders, sampling is hourly, DSN uses a fixed 10° mask). NASA has not published point coordinates for the regions, so each representative point is derived transparently from an IAU or published anchor and is labelled as not NASA-designated. Times are UTC throughout.
